aquaculture-s2.title: Wild catch and fish farming in one world region

table.caption: Production of fish and other aquatic animals in one region, million metric tons (invented data for practice)

items.q: Which is an example of aquaculture?
options: Raising salmon in net pens in a bay
Catching tuna with longlines at sea
Trawling the sea floor for shrimp
Fishing for trout with a rod in a river

why.correct: Aquaculture is farming fish in controlled conditions; the others catch wild fish.
options: Right: farmed fish in pens.
Longlining catches wild fish.
Trawling catches wild shrimp.
Sport fishing catches wild fish.

items.q: Which is a benefit of aquaculture compared with wild fishing?
options: It grows a lot of food on little space
It removes the need to give the fish any feed
It is unable to spread disease to any wild fish
It produces no waste in the water

why.correct: Farms grow fish densely and can reduce demand on wild fisheries.
options: Right: high yield on little space and less wild catch.
Many farmed fish are fed.
Open pens can spread disease to wild fish.
Farmed fish produce waste.

items.q: Waste from a crowded salmon pen collects on the sea floor below it. Why does the water near the bottom lose oxygen?
options: Decomposers use up oxygen breaking down waste
The waste blocks sunlight, so the sea floor heats up
The salmon breathe in the oxygen from the sea floor
The waste turns the salt water into fresh water

why.correct: Bacteria decomposing organic waste use oxygen in respiration, so dissolved oxygen falls.
options: Right: decomposition uses oxygen.
Shading would cool, not heat, and is not the cause.
The salmon are in the pen above, not on the bottom.
Waste does not change salinity like that.

items.q: Farmed salmon in net pens often carry sea lice, a parasite. Why is this a concern for wild salmon?
options: Young wild salmon swimming past can get lice
Sea lice from the pens make the wild salmon grow faster
Sea lice eat the waste under the pens and clean the water
Sea lice live on farmed salmon and stay inside the pens

why.correct: Crowded pens breed large numbers of lice, which spread to wild fish passing by.
options: Right: parasites spread from farms to wild fish.
Parasites harm their hosts.
Sea lice feed on fish, not waste.
Lice leave the pens and attach to wild fish.

items.q: Why does farming salmon do less to reduce pressure on wild fish than farming tilapia?
options: Salmon feed is made partly from wild fish
Salmon grow faster than tilapia, so more of them are farmed
Tilapia escape more often, so they replace wild fish in the sea
Salmon are farmed on land while tilapia are farmed in the sea

why.correct: Salmon are carnivores; their feed includes fish meal and oil from wild forage fish.
options: Right: carnivorous fish need wild fish in their feed.
Growth rate is not the reason.
Escapes are not what makes the difference here.
Salmon are mostly farmed in sea pens; tilapia mostly in ponds.

items.q: In parts of Southeast Asia, coastal shrimp farms were built by clearing mangrove forests. Which is a likely result?
options: Coasts lose storm protection and fish nurseries
Coasts gain storm protection because the ponds block waves
Wild fish catches rise because shrimp ponds feed them
Mangroves grow back inside the ponds within a year

why.correct: Mangroves shield coasts from storms and shelter young fish; clearing them removes both.
options: Right: lost storm protection and fish nurseries.
Ponds do not protect coasts like mangrove forests do.
Losing nursery habitat lowers wild catches.
Mangroves do not regrow in active ponds.

items.q: A fish farm produces 1,200 metric tons of salmon. It takes about 1.3 kg of feed to grow 1 kg of salmon. How many metric tons of feed does the farm use?

why.correct: $1{,}200\,\text{metric tons salmon} \times \frac{1.3\,\text{metric tons feed}}{1\,\text{metric ton salmon}} = 1{,}560$ metric tons of feed.

mistakes.why: It takes 1.3 kg of feed per kilogram of fish, so multiply by 1.3.

items.q: A town wants a fish farm in its bay but worries about pollution. Propose a farming method that would limit the harm and explain how it works.

why.correct: A method fitted to the town's concern, with its mechanism: raise the fish in closed tanks on land that filter and reuse water, which captures waste so it does not reach the bay.

solution.label: Method
options: raise the fish in closed tanks on land with filters
double the number of fish in each net pen
feed the fish more often in open pens

why.1: More crowding means more waste and disease.
why.2: More feed means more uneaten feed falling to the bottom.

mechanism.label: How it works
options: filters capture waste and the water is cleaned and reused
waste flows straight into the bay
wild fish eat all the waste

why.1: That is the problem the town wants to avoid.
why.2: Wild fish do not remove concentrated waste.

effect.label: Result
options: little waste reaches the bay and farmed fish cannot escape into it
more waste reaches the bay
the bay loses oxygen faster

why.1: Closed tanks keep waste out of the bay.
why.2: Less waste means less oxygen loss.

specific.model: The town could raise the fish in closed tanks on land with filters, which capture waste so the water is cleaned and reused. As a result little waste reaches the bay and farmed fish cannot escape into it.

items.q: In the diagram, what happens to waste and uneaten feed from the open net pen?
options: It sinks to the sea floor below the pen
It passes through a filter and is reused
It is eaten by the escaped fish
It floats to the surface and evaporates

why.correct: The arrow from the pen points down to the sea floor.
options: Right: it sinks below the pen.
The filter is part of the closed tank.
The diagram does not show escaped fish eating waste.
Waste does not evaporate.

items.q: Which problem shown for the open pen is solved by the closed tank design?
options: Farmed fish escaping into the wild
The cost of electricity for pumps
The need to feed the fish
The need to clean the water

why.correct: Fish in a tank on land cannot escape into the bay.
options: Right: no escapes from a tank on land.
Electricity cost is a drawback of the tank.
Tank fish still need feed.
The tank needs water cleaning (its filter).

items.q: Why are many fish farms still built as open pens even though closed tanks cause less pollution?
options: Open pens cost much less to build and run
Open pens produce no waste in the water
Closed tanks are unable to hold saltwater fish
Closed tanks spread more disease to wild fish

why.correct: Tanks need pumps, filters and electricity; pens use the sea for free.
options: Right: cost is the main reason.
Open pens do produce waste, as shown.
Saltwater fish can be raised in tanks.
Closed tanks keep disease away from wild fish.

items.q: Which trend does the table show from 1990 to 2022?
options: Aquaculture grew to 95 while wild capture stayed near 90
Wild capture grew from 85 to 95 million metric tons while aquaculture fell
Both wild capture and aquaculture fell between 1990 and 2022
Aquaculture stayed near 15 while wild capture grew to 95

why.correct: Aquaculture rose steadily; wild capture leveled off around 90 million metric tons.
options: Right: aquaculture grew about sixfold; capture leveled off.
Aquaculture rose sharply.
Aquaculture rose.
Aquaculture rose from 15 to 95.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in aquaculture production from 2000 to 2022, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, the 2000 production of 35.
That is 2022 as a percent of 2000 (271%). Percent change subtracts first.
60 million metric tons is the change. Divide by 35 and multiply by 100.
That is the change from 2022 back to 2000. Start from 2000.

items.q: In 2022, what percent of total production (wild capture plus aquaculture) came from aquaculture?

mistakes.why: Divide by the total, 90 + 95 = 185, not by wild capture alone.
48.6% is the share from wild capture. Aquaculture is 95 of 185.

items.q: In the table, wild capture has stayed near 90 million metric tons since 1990 while demand for fish grew. What does this suggest?
options: Wild fisheries are near their limit, so farming met the new demand
Wild fisheries could easily double their catch if more boats were built
Demand for fish has fallen, so farms are producing more than needed
Fish farming has caused wild fish stocks to grow much larger

why.correct: A flat wild catch as demand grew points to stocks at or past their limits; aquaculture filled the gap.
options: Right: the growth came from farming.
Many stocks are already fully fished or overfished.
Demand grew; total production rose.
Wild catch did not grow.

items.q: Which are drawbacks of open net-pen fish farming? Select all that apply.
options: Waste and uneaten feed pollute the water below the pens
Disease and parasites spread to wild fish
Farmed fish escape and compete with wild fish
Pens produce more bycatch than trawling
Pens raise the oxygen level of the bay
Pens use more fuel than fishing fleets

why.correct: Concentrated waste, disease and escapes are the main problems of open pens.
options: Right: concentrated waste.
Right: disease and parasites spread.
Right: escaped fish.
Farms do not use fishing gear, so they have no bycatch.
Decomposing waste lowers oxygen.
Farms usually use less fuel than fleets.
